newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Doctor gives gift of smile to children.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Doctor gives gift of smile to children.

text.p: He is the man behind the sweet first smiles of children all over the globe.

Dr. Ronald Zuker, head of plastic surgery at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, has pioneered a technique to give children afflicted with the extremely rare Moebius Syndrome the ability to do what they have never done before -- smile. His most famous patient, eight-year-old Palmdale, California, schoolgirl Chelsey Thomas, beamed with delight for the first time in her life in early June after winning the attention of the world as "the girl who couldn't smile."

Moebius Sydrome, an illness caused early in fetal development, inhibits development of nerves, and hence muscles, in the face. Babies with Moebius have trouble sucking and swallowing and often have shortened or webbed fingers. They grow into children who often drool, have trouble closing their mouths and eyes, may have weak eye muscles and, most importantly, have faces devoid of any expression.
They are judged harshly by the world.

"If they can't smile, they are often misinterpreted as stupid, because they are not reacting to what somebody is saying, or as being uninterested, or as being arrogant, or mean, mad, unhappy," Zuker, who has helped more than 30 Moebius sufferers, told Reuters.

"You know that when people smile back, when you see somebody smile, you get a warm feeling. If they can't do that, then their relationship with that other person, or any other person, is hindered. They don't have that same warmth."
Zuker is warmth personified. Fresh from surgery and still clad in his surgical greens and cap, he describes the plight of the children who cannot smile with sensitivity and empathy.

Smiling is one of those abilities we take for granted. It is the first way we interact with the world -- a baby can lift its lips in a smile at just a few weeks old, before it gets control of most of its other tiny muscles.

In "The Merchant of Venice", Shakespeare pinpoints the importance of a smile to the perception of a person by his peers: "And other of such vinegar aspect/ That they'll not show their teeth in way of smile, /Though Nestor swear the jest be laughable."

Moebius is an extremely rare condition, affecting about one in two million people, Zuker said. Many never know why they cannot animate their faces nor that there are others like them in the world. Zuker gives these children their smiles by transplanting part of a muscle from the inside of the thigh into the face and attaching it to the nerve that goes into the masseter or "biting" muscle in the jaw, which is present in most Moebius sufferers.

Zuker's office walls are filled with diplomas and certificates proclaiming his international training. These sit incongruously above wicker shelves stacked with toys. His pleasantly cluttered desk is backed by photos of children all over the world his pioneering surgical techniques have helped.

But the most famous thus far is Chelsey Thomas. The international attention her case attracted forced Zuker to operate under the glare of a media spotlight. But the fact that he developed the technique went largely unmentioned by reports on Chelsey's progress.

"When you do a case like Chelsey Thomas with the world watching and cameras all around, it's tense. These procedures are extremely difficult, very demanding technically, because every step has to be done exactly," Zuker said.

He concedes that the publicity the case received had a vital fringe benefit -- it let many people who had Moebius and never knew what their disorder was know there are others like them and that there is a treatment available.

Janine Hutchinson of Calgary, Alberta, was one of those who saw Chelsey's story on television. Her mother, Darlene Boyce, 28, said the television report gave her hope. "I was absolutely floored because I had never heard tell of, met, seen anyone else with Moebius syndrome," she said.

Boyce saw the Chelsey Thomas report in December, made several calls in an effort to track down the name of the doctor who performed the surgery and discovered to her delight that he was Canadian. This meant that all of Janine's operations were covered by the government healthcare plan.

Things progressed quickly after that. Janine had the first half of her face done on April 30 and was smiling a full half-smile by mid-June. She left Toronto's Sick Children's Hospital recently after her second operation and Boyce is confident she will be able to look suitably delighted about her eighth birthday gifts on Dec. 23rd.
Janine, 7, said she and other children with Moebius want to smile "so adults don't look funny when they grow up."
